java-basics-001.explanation: **The problem:** Java promises "write once, run anywhere," but your machine's CPU only understands its own native instructions — not Java. **Why it works:** `javac` compiles your `.java` source into platform-neutral **bytecode** (`.class` files). The **JVM** is a program that reads that bytecode and executes it on the current OS/CPU, so the same `.class` runs on Windows, macOS, or Linux as long as a JVM exists there. **The three layers:** the **JVM** executes bytecode; the **JRE** bundles the JVM with the standard class libraries (`java.util`, `java.io`, …) so programs can actually do useful work; the **JDK** adds the compiler and tooling so you can build programs in the first place. **Common mistakes:** installing only a JRE and wondering why `javac` isn't found — you need the JDK to compile. Modern downloads (JDK 11+) usually ship the JDK and you rarely install a standalone JRE anymore.

java-basics-002.explanation: **The problem:** When you run `java MyApp`, the JVM needs one well-known method to start at — but it can't create an object first (which constructor? what arguments?). **Why this signature:** `static` means the method belongs to the class itself, so the JVM can invoke `MyApp.main(...)` with no instance. `public` lets the JVM (outside your class) call it. `void` because there's no caller to receive a return value — use `System.exit(code)` for exit status. `String[] args` carries whatever you typed after the class name on the command line. **Why it works:** the JVM reflectively looks up this precise shape; the parameter may also be written `String... args` (varargs) and the name `args` is just convention. **Common mistakes:** forgetting `static` (compiles fine, then "Error: Main method not found"), or typing `String args` instead of `String[] args`.

java-basics-003.explanation: **The problem:** New Java developers often assume `String` is a primitive like in some languages — it isn't. **The eight primitives:** integer types `byte` (8-bit), `short` (16), `int` (32, the default for whole numbers), `long` (64, suffix `L`); floating-point `float` (32, suffix `f`) and `double` (64, the default for decimals); `char` (a single 16-bit Unicode unit, single quotes); and `boolean` (`true`/`false`). **Why it matters:** primitives hold their value directly (fast, no `null`), while everything else — `String`, arrays, your own classes — is a **reference type** that holds a pointer to an object on the heap and can be `null`. **Common mistakes:** using `==` to compare `String`s (that compares references — use `.equals`); writing `float x = 1.5;` without the `f` suffix (1.5 is a `double`, won't fit) — write `1.5f`; and forgetting `long big = 3000000000L;` needs the `L` or it overflows `int`.
java-basics-003.example:
```java
byte    b = 100;
short   s = 30000;
int     i = 42;          // default for integers
long    big = 9_000_000_000L; // L suffix; underscores allowed for readability
float   f = 1.5f;        // f suffix required
double  d = 3.14159;     // default for decimals
char    c = 'A';         // single quotes, one Unicode unit
boolean flag = true;

String  name = "Ana";   // NOT a primitive — a class instance
```

java-basics-004.explanation: **The problem:** `a = b` does very different things depending on whether the variables are primitives or objects, and this surprises beginners. **Why it happens:** a primitive variable is a box containing the actual value; copying it copies the value. A reference variable is a box containing the *address* of an object on the heap; copying it copies the address, so both variables now point at the **same** object. **Why it matters:** mutating the object through one reference is visible through the other — but reassigning one reference doesn't affect the other. Also, only reference types can hold `null` ("points at nothing"), which is why dereferencing a `null` throws `NullPointerException`. **Common mistakes:** expecting changes to a copied object not to be visible (they are — same object); and confusing reassignment (`b = new ...`) with mutation (`b.setX(...)`).

java-basics-005.explanation: **The problem:** Java's collections and generics work only with objects (reference types), but you constantly want to store `int`s, `double`s, etc. **Why wrappers exist:** each primitive has a class counterpart — `Integer`, `Long`, `Double`, `Boolean`, `Character`, `Byte`, `Short`, `Float` — that wraps the value in an object. **How autoboxing helps:** since Java 5 the compiler auto-inserts the conversion, so `list.add(5)` boxes `5` into `Integer.valueOf(5)`, and `int n = list.get(0)` unboxes it back. **Common mistakes:** (1) **NullPointerException on unboxing** — if an `Integer` is `null`, `int n = obj` throws, because there's no value to unbox. (2) **Comparing wrappers with `==`** compares references, not values; use `.equals()` or unbox first. (3) Autoboxing in a tight loop creates many objects — fine usually, but prefer primitives in hot numeric code.

java-basics-006.explanation: **The problem:** Java is verbose — `Map<String, List<Integer>> m = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();` repeats the type twice. **What `var` does:** introduced in Java 10, it asks the compiler to infer the variable's type from the right-hand side. The variable is still **strongly, statically typed** — `var` is not dynamic and not `Object`; the inferred type is locked in at compile time. **Why it works:** the initializer unambiguously determines the type, so the compiler fills it in. **Where you can use it:** local variables *with an initializer*, and loop variables. **Where you cannot:** fields, method parameters, return types, or a `var x;` with no initializer (nothing to infer from), or `var x = null` (ambiguous). **Common mistakes:** overusing it where it hurts readability (e.g. `var x = getThing();` hides the type) — prefer it when the type is obvious from the right side.

java-basics-007.explanation: **The problem:** `7 / 2` giving `3` instead of `3.5` is a classic surprise that causes subtle bugs in calculations. **Why it happens:** in Java the result type of an operator depends on its operands. `int / int` produces an `int`, so the fractional part is **truncated** (toward zero, not rounded) — `7 / 2` is `3`, `-7 / 2` is `-3`. **Why the fix works:** if at least one operand is `double` (or `float`), Java *promotes* the other to floating point and does floating-point division. **How to fix:** make one operand a decimal literal (`7 / 2.0`), or cast (`(double) 7 / 2`). **Common mistakes:** casting too late — `(double)(7 / 2)` is `3.0`, because the integer division already happened *before* the cast. Cast an operand, not the result. Also `%` (remainder) follows the same int/double rules: `7 % 2` is `1`.
java-basics-007.example:
```java
System.out.println(7 / 2);          // 3   (int division, truncated)
System.out.println(7 / 2.0);        // 3.5 (one operand is double)
System.out.println((double) 7 / 2); // 3.5 (cast an operand first)
System.out.println((double)(7 / 2));// 3.0 (too late — already truncated)
System.out.println(7 % 2);          // 1   (remainder)
```

java-basics-008.explanation: **The problem:** index-based loops are noisy and a common source of off-by-one and `IndexOutOfBoundsException` bugs when you only want the elements. **What for-each does:** `for (Type item : iterable)` walks every element of any array or `Iterable` (List, Set, …) in order, with no counter to mismanage. **Why it works:** the compiler turns it into an iterator (for collections) or index walk (for arrays) behind the scenes. **When to use the classic for:** you need the index, you iterate backwards, you step by more than one, or you remove elements while iterating (removing inside a for-each throws `ConcurrentModificationException` — use an explicit `Iterator.remove()` instead). **Common mistakes:** trying to modify the collection's structure during a for-each; and expecting to change array elements via the loop variable — reassigning `item` doesn't write back to the array (use the index for that).

java-oop-001.explanation: **The problem:** beginners conflate the definition of a thing with an actual thing. **The distinction:** a **class** is the design — it lists what fields each instance will have and what methods they can run, but it holds no per-object data itself. An **object** is what you get when you `new` the class: a live instance on the heap with its own field values. **Why it works:** `new Dog()` allocates memory, runs the constructor, and returns a reference to that instance; each `new` produces a separate object, so two `Dog`s can have different names. **Common mistakes:** putting data that should be per-object into `static` fields (then all instances share it — see static vs instance); and thinking the class "runs" — only objects (or static members) do. A useful mantra: the class is the noun's *definition*; objects are the nouns.

java-oop-002.explanation: **The problem:** if any code can read and write an object's fields directly, you can't enforce rules (a bank balance going negative) and you can never change the internals without breaking callers. **What encapsulation does:** mark fields `private` so only the class itself touches them, and expose a *deliberate* public surface (methods) that guards every change. **The four access levels:** `private` (this class only), *package-private* (no keyword — same package), `protected` (package + subclasses), `public` (everyone). **Why it works:** callers depend on your methods, not your fields, so you can validate inputs and later swap the implementation freely. **Common mistakes:** auto-generating a public getter+setter for every field (that's barely better than public fields) — only expose what callers genuinely need, and put validation/behavior in methods rather than leaking raw state.

java-oop-003.explanation: **The problem:** objects often need valid starting state, and forgetting how default constructors work causes confusing "constructor not found" errors. **What a constructor is:** a special initializer with the class's exact name and no return type, run once by `new`. You can overload it (several constructors with different parameters) and chain with `this(...)`. **The default rule:** if you declare *no* constructor, the compiler silently adds a public no-arg one so `new Foo()` works. The moment you write *any* constructor, that freebie disappears — so if you only wrote `Foo(int x)`, then `new Foo()` no longer compiles unless you add it back. **Why it works:** the compiler only fills the gap when you've provided nothing. **Common mistakes:** assuming a no-arg constructor always exists (frameworks/`new Foo()` may need one — add it explicitly); and shadowing fields without `this` (`name = name` assigns the parameter to itself — use `this.name = name`).

java-oop-004.explanation: **The problem:** related classes often share behavior, and copy-pasting it duplicates bugs. **What inheritance does:** `class Dog extends Animal` makes `Dog` an `Animal` — it inherits `Animal`'s non-private members and can add or override behavior. **Constructors and `super`:** a subclass object *is* a superclass object underneath, so the superclass part must be initialized first. The compiler inserts an implicit `super()` (no-arg) as the first line of every subclass constructor unless you call `super(args)` yourself; if the superclass has no no-arg constructor, you *must* call `super(args)` explicitly. `super.foo()` reaches the parent's version of an overridden method. **Why single inheritance:** Java allows only one direct superclass (to avoid the diamond problem) but a class can implement many interfaces. **Common mistakes:** expecting to inherit `private` members (you don't — use `protected` or the parent's public API); and overusing inheritance where composition ("has-a") fits better than "is-a".

java-oop-005.explanation: **The problem:** you want one piece of code (e.g. a loop over `List<Animal>`) to do the right thing for each concrete type without `if/else` on the type. **What polymorphism does:** when a subclass **overrides** a method, calling it through a superclass reference runs the *subclass's* implementation, decided by the object's real type at runtime — this is **dynamic dispatch** (a.k.a. late/virtual binding). **Why it works:** the variable's *declared* type decides which methods you may call (compile-time), but the *object's* type decides which override actually runs (runtime). **Why it's powerful:** you program to the abstraction (`Animal`, an interface) and add new subclasses without touching the calling code — the open/closed principle. **Common mistakes:** confusing it with overloading (overloading is resolved by argument types at compile time, not by the object's runtime type); forgetting `@Override` (so a typo silently creates a *new* method instead of overriding); and that `static` and `private` methods are *not* polymorphic.

java-oop-006.explanation: **The problem:** the two words look alike and beginners mix them up, but they are unrelated mechanisms. **Overloading:** several methods in the *same* class share a name but differ in parameter list (count or types). The compiler picks which one to call based on the *arguments at the call site* — this is **static/compile-time** resolution. Return type alone can't distinguish overloads. **Overriding:** a *subclass* provides a new body for an inherited method with the *same* signature; the JVM picks the version based on the object's *runtime* type (polymorphism). **Why it works:** overloading is just a naming convenience; overriding is the engine of dynamic dispatch. **Common mistakes:** thinking changing only the return type overloads a method (it doesn't compile); and forgetting `@Override` so a mismatched signature accidentally *overloads* instead of overrides, and your method never gets called polymorphically.

java-oop-007.explanation: **The problem:** sometimes a base type is meaningful as a concept but has no sensible standalone instance — a generic `Shape` has no area until it's a `Circle` or `Square`. **What abstract gives you:** mark the class `abstract` so `new Shape()` is forbidden, and mark methods that every subclass *must* define as `abstract` (no body). The class can still hold concrete fields and fully-implemented helper methods that all subclasses inherit. **Why it works:** the compiler forces each concrete subclass to implement every abstract method, guaranteeing the contract while letting the base supply shared code. **Abstract class vs interface:** use an abstract class when subclasses share *state* and *implementation*, not just a contract. **Common mistakes:** trying to instantiate an abstract class; and forgetting that a subclass which doesn't implement *all* abstract methods must itself be declared `abstract`.

java-oop-008.explanation: **The problem:** you want unrelated classes to be usable interchangeably based on *what they can do*, not their inheritance chain. **What an interface is:** a named set of method signatures (a contract). A class declares `implements Foo` and must provide every method, after which it can be used wherever a `Foo` is expected. **Why it's powerful:** a class can implement *many* interfaces (Java forbids multiple class inheritance but not multiple interface implementation), and code depending on the interface doesn't care which concrete class it gets — that's loose coupling, and it's what makes mocking/testing and swapping implementations easy. **Modern features:** interface methods are implicitly `public abstract`; constants are `public static final`; since Java 8 interfaces may add `default` methods (with a body) and `static` methods. **Common mistakes:** forgetting interface methods are public (you can't reduce visibility in the implementer); and reaching for an abstract class when you only need a contract (no shared state) — prefer an interface.

java-oop-009.explanation: **The problem:** both can declare methods subclasses must implement, so it's unclear which to reach for. **The deciding factors:** (1) **Multiple inheritance** — a class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class, so a capability that cross-cuts unrelated types must be an interface. (2) **State** — abstract classes can have instance fields and constructors; interfaces cannot hold instance state (only constants). (3) **Shared implementation** — abstract classes are the natural home for common concrete code; interfaces can add `default` methods but those can't use instance fields. **Rule of thumb:** model a *capability* ("is comparable", "is runnable") as an interface; model a closely-related *family with shared data/behavior* as an abstract class. **Why it works:** interfaces maximize flexibility and decoupling; abstract classes maximize code reuse within one hierarchy. **Common mistakes:** using an abstract class purely for a contract (locks subclasses out of other parents); and cramming state into interfaces via hacks. Modern Java often favors interfaces + composition.

java-oop-010.explanation: **The problem:** not everything belongs to an object — `Math.sqrt` needs no `Math` instance, and a shared counter shouldn't be duplicated per object. **What `static` means:** the member belongs to the *class*, so there is exactly one copy regardless of how many objects exist, and you access it via the class name. **Instance members** belong to each object — every `new` gets its own copy of the fields. **Why it works:** static members exist as soon as the class loads, before any object is created, which is exactly why a static method can't use `this` or read instance fields (there's no particular object). **When to use static:** stateless utility methods, constants (`static final`), and genuinely class-wide state like a counter or cache. **Common mistakes:** making everything static (kills polymorphism and testability — statics aren't overridable); and accidental shared state — a `static` field is shared by *all* instances, so mutating it from one object affects them all.

java-oop-011.explanation: **The problem:** you sometimes want to guarantee something won't change — a constant, an un-overridable method, an un-subclassable class. **The three uses:** (1) `final` **variable** can be assigned exactly once; combined with `static` it's the idiom for constants (`static final double PI`). (2) `final` **method** can't be overridden, locking in critical behavior. (3) `final` **class** can't be subclassed (e.g. `String`, `Integer`), which also helps make a class immutable and secure. **The key subtlety:** for a reference variable, `final` freezes the *reference*, not the *object*. `final List<String> xs = new ArrayList<>();` still allows `xs.add("a")` — you just can't do `xs = somethingElse`. **Why it works:** the compiler enforces single assignment and the JVM/compiler block overriding/extension. **Common mistakes:** thinking `final` makes the pointed-at object immutable (it doesn't); and that `final` on a parameter only stops reassigning the parameter, not mutating what it refers to.

java-oop-012.explanation: **The problem:** you give a class a meaningful `equals` (two `Point`s are equal if x and y match), put it in a `HashSet`/`HashMap`, and lookups mysteriously fail. **Why it happens:** hash collections first compute `hashCode()` to pick a bucket, then use `equals()` only among items in that bucket. The default `hashCode()` (from `Object`) is based on object identity, so two logically-equal objects get *different* hash codes, land in *different* buckets, and are never compared — the set thinks they're distinct and `get` returns `null`. **The contract:** if `a.equals(b)` is true, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` *must* hold (the reverse need not). **Why the fix works:** overriding both so equal objects hash the same routes them to the same bucket where `equals` can confirm the match. **Common mistakes:** overriding only one of the two; and including mutable fields in `equals`/`hashCode` then mutating a key already in a map (it becomes unfindable). Use `Objects.equals`/`Objects.hash` to implement both correctly.

java-str-001.explanation: **The problem:** beginners call `s.trim()` or `s.replace(...)` and are confused that `s` is unchanged. **What immutable means:** once a `String` exists, its contents are fixed forever. Every "modifying" method actually builds and returns a *brand-new* `String`, leaving the original alone. **Why Java does this:** immutable strings can be safely shared across threads without locking, cached/interned in the **string pool** (so identical literals reuse one object), and used as reliable `HashMap` keys (their hash never changes). **Why the fix works:** to keep a change you must reassign — `s = s.trim();` — capturing the new object. **Common mistakes:** discarding the return value (`s.toUpperCase();` does nothing); and building strings by `+=` in a loop, which creates a new object each iteration (O(n²)) — use `StringBuilder` for that.
java-str-001.example:
```java
String s = "  hello  ";
s.trim();                 // result thrown away — s unchanged
System.out.println("[" + s + "]"); // [  hello  ]

s = s.trim();             // capture the new String
System.out.println("[" + s + "]"); // [hello]

String up = s.toUpperCase(); // new String; s still "hello"
```

java-str-002.explanation: **The problem:** `a == b` sometimes appears to work for strings (because of the string pool) and then suddenly fails, causing intermittent bugs. **Why it happens:** `==` on reference types tests whether both variables point to the *same object*. String *literals* are interned in a shared pool, so `"hi" == "hi"` may be `true` — but a string built at runtime (`new String("hi")`, concatenation, user input) is a different object, so `==` is `false` even when the text matches. **Why `.equals` works:** `String` overrides `equals` to compare contents character by character. **Best practices:** use `.equals`; for case-insensitive use `.equalsIgnoreCase`; to avoid NPE when one side might be null, call it on a known-non-null literal (`"yes".equals(input)`) or use `Objects.equals(a, b)`. `compareTo` returns an `int` (<0, 0, >0) for ordering, not a boolean. **Common mistakes:** using `==`; and calling `.equals` on a possibly-null reference.

java-str-003.explanation: **The problem:** assembling a string in a loop with `result += part` gets slow for large inputs. **Why it happens:** strings are immutable, so each `+=` allocates a new `String` and copies all existing characters — over n iterations that's O(n²) copying and lots of garbage. **What StringBuilder does:** it holds a *mutable* char buffer; `append` writes into it (growing the buffer occasionally), so building the whole string is O(n). Call `toString()` once at the end. **When NOT to bother:** for a fixed handful of concatenations, plain `+` is clearer and the compiler already compiles it efficiently (often into a StringBuilder for you). The rule is: *loops and dynamic assembly → StringBuilder; simple one-liners → `+`.* **Common mistakes:** using `StringBuilder` everywhere (premature, hurts readability); forgetting `toString()`; and `StringBuffer` — it's the older thread-safe (synchronized, slower) version; prefer `StringBuilder` unless you truly share it across threads.

java-col-001.explanation: **The problem:** plain arrays have a fixed size you must know up front, hold no convenience methods, and can't easily grow. **What a List gives you:** `List<E>` is the interface for an ordered, indexable, *resizable* sequence; `ArrayList<E>` is the default implementation backed by a growable array. You get `add`, `remove`, `get`, `size`, `contains`, iteration, etc., and generics keep it type-safe (`List<String>` only holds Strings). **Why program to `List`:** declaring `List<String> xs = new ArrayList<>();` lets you swap the implementation later without changing callers. **Performance shape:** `get`/`set` by index are O(1); `add` at the end is amortized O(1); inserting/removing in the middle is O(n) (shifts elements). **Common mistakes:** trying to store primitives directly (use wrappers — `List<Integer>`, autoboxing helps); and using `Arrays.asList(...)` then calling `add`/`remove` on it (that returns a *fixed-size* view and throws) — wrap it in `new ArrayList<>(...)` if you need to modify it.

java-col-002.explanation: **The problem:** both implement `List`, so it's tempting to think they're interchangeable — but their performance profiles differ. **ArrayList** stores elements in a contiguous backing array: `get(i)`/`set(i)` are O(1), iteration is cache-friendly and fast, and appending is amortized O(1). Its weakness is inserting/removing in the *middle* (O(n) to shift). **LinkedList** is a doubly-linked chain of nodes: inserting/removing at a node you already hold (e.g. the ends, via `Deque` operations) is O(1), but `get(i)` is O(n) because it must walk from an end, and it uses more memory per element (two pointers per node) with poor cache locality. **The practical answer:** default to `ArrayList`; it wins for random access and is usually faster overall even for many mid-list operations because of memory locality. Reach for `LinkedList` only when you genuinely need queue/deque behavior at the ends. **Common mistakes:** choosing `LinkedList` for index-heavy code; and indexing a `LinkedList` in a loop (turns an O(n) loop into O(n²)).

java-col-003.explanation: **The problem:** you need a collection of *unique* things and fast "have I seen this?" checks, which a `List` does poorly (`contains` is O(n) and duplicates slip in). **What a Set gives you:** it rejects duplicates (`add` returns `false` if already present) and offers fast membership tests. **HashSet** uses hashing for O(1) average `add`/`contains`/`remove` but gives **no order** guarantee. Variants: **LinkedHashSet** preserves insertion order; **TreeSet** keeps elements sorted (O(log n), requires `Comparable`/`Comparator`). **Why it works:** like `HashMap`, `HashSet` relies on `hashCode()`/`equals()` to detect duplicates — so for your own classes you must override both or duplicates won't be caught. **Common mistakes:** depending on `HashSet` iteration order (undefined); expecting indexed access (`set.get(0)` doesn't exist); and storing mutable objects whose hash changes after insertion (they become unfindable).

java-col-004.explanation: **The problem:** you need to associate values with lookup keys (username → user, word → count) with fast retrieval. **What a Map is:** a collection of key→value entries with *unique keys*; `HashMap` gives O(1) average `put`/`get`/`containsKey`. `put` on an existing key overwrites the old value and returns it; `get` on a missing key returns `null`. **Iteration:** `keySet()`, `values()`, and `entrySet()` (iterate entries to get key and value together — the efficient way). **Useful helpers:** `getOrDefault(k, d)`, `putIfAbsent`, `computeIfAbsent`, and `merge` (great for counting). **Why it works:** keys are hashed to buckets, relying on the key's `hashCode()`/`equals()` — so mutable or improperly-implemented keys break lookups. **Variants:** `LinkedHashMap` (insertion order), `TreeMap` (sorted keys). **Common mistakes:** treating a `null` from `get` as "key absent" when the stored value itself might be `null` (use `containsKey`); and using mutable objects as keys.

java-col-005.explanation: **The problem:** the naive count loop needs a null check every time (`if (map.containsKey(k)) ... else ...`), which is verbose and error-prone. **The idioms:** (1) `getOrDefault` — `map.put(k, map.getOrDefault(k, 0) + 1)` reads the current count (or 0) and writes back the increment. (2) `merge` — `map.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)` says "if k is absent, store 1; otherwise replace the value with sum(old, 1)". (3) `computeIfAbsent` shines for map-of-lists: `map.computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new ArrayList<>()).add(item)`. **Why merge works:** it folds the absent/present cases into one call, eliminating the branch and the boxing pitfalls. **Common mistakes:** `map.get(k) + 1` when `k` is absent throws NPE (unboxing `null`) — that's exactly what `getOrDefault`/`merge` avoid; and recomputing the lookup twice (get then put) when `merge` does it in one.

java-col-006.explanation: **The problem:** picking the wrong collection leads to duplicates you didn't want, missing order, or slow lookups. **The mental model:** **List** = ordered sequence, *allows duplicates*, indexable (`ArrayList`). **Set** = *no duplicates*, membership-focused, not indexable (`HashSet` unordered, `LinkedHashSet` insertion order, `TreeSet` sorted). **Map** = key→value with *unique keys* (`HashMap` unordered, `LinkedHashMap` insertion order, `TreeMap` sorted keys). **Why the wrong options are wrong:** a `List` *does* allow duplicates and *does* preserve insertion order; a plain `HashMap`/`HashSet` makes *no* ordering promise — relying on its iteration order is a classic bug. **How to choose:** need order + duplicates + index → List; need uniqueness → Set; need lookup by key → Map; need sorting → the Tree* variant. **Common mistakes:** assuming HashMap/HashSet are ordered; and using a List with `contains` for uniqueness (O(n)) when a Set is the right tool.

java-exc-001.explanation: **The problem:** Java sometimes *forces* you to handle an exception and sometimes doesn't, which is confusing until you see the hierarchy. **The hierarchy:** everything throwable is a `Throwable`, split into `Error` (JVM-level, don't catch — e.g. `OutOfMemoryError`) and `Exception`. Within `Exception`, `RuntimeException` and its subclasses are **unchecked**; all *other* `Exception` subclasses are **checked**. **Checked** (e.g. `IOException`, `SQLException`) represent recoverable external conditions; the compiler insists you either `catch` them or declare `throws`. **Unchecked** (e.g. `NullPointerException`, `IllegalArgumentException`, `IndexOutOfBoundsException`) usually mean a *bug* in your code — the compiler doesn't force handling because the right fix is to correct the code. **Why the design:** checked exceptions document and enforce failure modes a caller can reasonably handle. **Common mistakes:** catching exceptions just to silence the compiler (`catch (Exception e) {}` swallows real bugs); wrapping everything in `RuntimeException` to dodge `throws`; and catching `Error`.

java-exc-002.explanation: **The problem:** cleanup code (close a file, release a lock) must run whether or not an exception was thrown — duplicating it in both the success and failure paths is fragile. **What finally does:** the `finally` block executes after `try`/`catch` *no matter how* the block exits — normal completion, a caught or uncaught exception, or even a `return` inside `try`/`catch`. That makes it the reliable home for cleanup. **Why it works:** the JVM guarantees the `finally` runs during unwinding before control leaves the method. **The footguns:** a `return` or `throw` *inside* `finally` overrides whatever the `try`/`catch` was returning/throwing — silently swallowing the original exception, so never `return`/`throw` from `finally`. **The exceptions to "always":** `System.exit()` or a JVM crash skips it. **Modern preference:** for closing resources, **try-with-resources** is cleaner and avoids manual `finally` + null checks. **Common mistakes:** returning from `finally`; and forgetting that `finally` runs even after a `try` `return` (it can change the result).

java-exc-003.explanation: **The problem:** the old pattern — open a resource, use it in `try`, close it in `finally` — is verbose, easy to get wrong (null checks, close() itself throwing), and a frequent source of leaks. **What try-with-resources does:** declare resources in the `try (...)` header; any object implementing `AutoCloseable` (files, streams, JDBC connections, …) is closed automatically when the block exits — whether normally or via exception — in *reverse* order of declaration. **Why it works:** the compiler generates the `finally`-and-close logic for you, including correctly handling an exception thrown by `close()` itself (it's attached as a *suppressed* exception rather than masking the original). **Why prefer it:** less code, no leaks, correct exception semantics. **Common mistakes:** still writing manual `finally { x.close(); }` (use this instead); declaring a resource that isn't `AutoCloseable`; and reusing a resource variable after the block (it's already closed).

java-exc-004.explanation: **The problem:** the two keywords differ by one letter and do completely different things. **`throw`** is a *statement* that raises an exception *right now*: `throw new IllegalStateException("bad");` — it stops normal flow and starts unwinding the stack looking for a `catch`. **`throws`** is part of a *method's declaration* that lists which **checked** exceptions the method may let propagate to its caller: `void load() throws IOException`. **Why both exist:** `throw` is the action; `throws` is the contract that the compiler uses to enforce catch-or-declare for checked exceptions. **Why it works:** declaring `throws IOException` lets you `throw` (or call something that throws) a checked `IOException` without catching it locally — the obligation moves to the caller. **Common mistakes:** writing `throws` when you mean `throw` (and vice versa); declaring `throws` for unchecked exceptions (legal but pointless — the compiler doesn't require it); and over-broad `throws Exception` that hides what can really go wrong.

java-exc-005.explanation: **The problem:** throwing generic `Exception`/`RuntimeException` forces callers to catch everything and loses meaning about *what* went wrong. **What a custom exception gives you:** a named type (`InsufficientFundsException`) that callers can catch *specifically*, carrying domain-relevant data and a clear message. **How to write one:** extend `RuntimeException` (unchecked — for programming errors or when you don't want to force handling) or `Exception` (checked — when callers should recover); add constructors that forward a message and an optional `cause` to `super(...)`. **Why preserve the cause:** passing the original exception as the cause keeps the full stack trace when you wrap a low-level error in a domain one. **Why it works:** the type hierarchy lets `catch (InsufficientFundsException e)` match only that case. **Common mistakes:** swallowing the original cause when wrapping (always pass it to `super`); creating a checked exception that callers can't actually recover from (prefer unchecked then); and making dozens of near-identical exception classes.

java-gen-001.explanation: **The problem:** pre-generics collections stored `Object`, so you could accidentally put a `String` into a list meant for `Integer`s, and every read needed a manual cast that could blow up with `ClassCastException` at runtime. **What generics do:** they let a type or method take a *type parameter* — `List<String>` — checked by the compiler. The compiler rejects adding the wrong type and lets `get()` return the right type with no cast. **Why it works:** all the checking happens at *compile* time; at runtime the type parameter is erased (type erasure), so there's no per-object overhead. **The payoff:** bugs that were runtime `ClassCastException`s become compile errors. **Common mistakes:** using *raw types* (`List` without `<>`), which disables the checks and brings back the old dangers; and confusing generics with arrays (arrays are covariant and check at runtime; generics are invariant and check at compile time).

java-gen-002.explanation: **The problem:** you want one class or method to work for *any* type without duplicating code or losing type safety. **Generic class:** put type parameters in angle brackets after the class name — `class Box<T>` — and use `T` as a stand-in type for fields, parameters, and return types. The caller picks the type: `new Box<String>()`. **Generic method:** declare the type parameter *before the return type* — `static <T> T first(List<T> xs)` — so the method introduces its own type variable independent of the class. The compiler usually *infers* `T` from the arguments, so you rarely specify it explicitly. **Why it works:** the compiler substitutes the concrete type at each call site and checks everything, then erases it. **Conventions:** `T`/`E`/`K`/`V`/`R`. **Common mistakes:** forgetting the `<T>` before the return type on a generic method; trying to do `new T()` or `T.class` (erased — not allowed); and creating generic arrays (`new T[]`) which the language forbids.

java-gen-003.explanation: **The problem:** generics are *invariant* — a `List<Integer>` is NOT a `List<Number>` — which blocks flexible method signatures like "sum any list of numbers." **What wildcards do:** `? extends T` means "some unknown type that *is a* T" (upper bound) and `? super T` means "some unknown type that T *is a*" (lower bound). **PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super:** if the structure *produces* values you'll read as `T`, use `? extends T` (you can read them as `T`, but can't safely add anything because the exact subtype is unknown). If it *consumes* values you'll write, use `? super T` (you can add `T` and its subtypes, but reads come back only as `Object`). **Why it works:** the bounds tell the compiler exactly which operations stay type-safe given the uncertainty. **Common mistakes:** trying to `add` to a `? extends` collection (rejected); expecting typed reads from a `? super` collection (they're `Object`); and reaching for wildcards when a simple generic method type parameter would be clearer.

java-mod-001.explanation: **The problem:** passing a small piece of behavior (a comparator, a click handler) used to require a bulky anonymous inner class — lots of boilerplate for one method. **What a lambda is:** a compact literal for an anonymous function, `(args) -> expressionOrBlock`. **What it targets:** a **functional interface** — any interface with exactly one abstract method (`Runnable`, `Comparator`, `Function`, `Predicate`, …). The lambda *is* an implementation of that single method; the compiler infers parameter types from the interface. **Why it works:** `Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("hi");` is shorthand for an anonymous class implementing `run()`. Single-expression bodies return implicitly; block bodies use `{ }` and explicit `return`. **Why it matters:** behavior becomes a value you can store, pass, and compose — the basis of the Streams API. **Common mistakes:** lambdas can only capture *effectively final* local variables (you can't reassign a captured local); and `this` inside a lambda refers to the *enclosing* instance, not the lambda (unlike anonymous classes).

java-mod-002.explanation: **The problem:** lambdas need a *type* — Java is statically typed, so `() -> ...` must correspond to some interface. **What a functional interface is:** an interface with exactly **one abstract method** (SAM — Single Abstract Method). That single method is what a lambda or method reference implements. `default` and `static` methods don't count, so an interface can have many of those and still be functional. **The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation** is optional but makes the compiler *enforce* the one-abstract-method rule, catching accidental additions. **The built-in toolkit (`java.util.function`):** `Function<T,R>` (T→R), `Predicate<T>` (T→boolean), `Consumer<T>` (T→void), `Supplier<T>` (()→T), `BiFunction`, `UnaryOperator`, plus classics `Runnable` and `Comparator`. **Why it works:** these standard types mean you rarely write your own; APIs accept them so any lambda fits. **Common mistakes:** writing custom interfaces when a built-in fits; and adding a second abstract method (breaks lambda compatibility — `@FunctionalInterface` would flag it).

java-mod-003.explanation: **The problem:** loops that filter-map-collect are verbose and mix *what* you want with *how* to iterate. **What streams do:** they let you express a data pipeline declaratively — `source.stream().filter(...).map(...).collect(...)` — reading like the transformation itself. **Two operation kinds:** **intermediate** ops (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`) are *lazy* — they just build the pipeline and return a new stream, doing no work yet. **Terminal** ops (`collect`, `forEach`, `count`, `reduce`, `findFirst`, `anyMatch`) *trigger* execution and produce a result or side effect. **Why laziness matters:** the pipeline is fused into a single pass and can short-circuit (e.g. `findFirst` stops early), so it's efficient. **One-shot:** a stream is consumed by its terminal op and can't be reused — create a new one from the source. **Common mistakes:** expecting intermediate ops to run without a terminal (nothing happens); reusing a consumed stream (IllegalStateException); and side-effecting inside `map`/`filter` (keep them pure; use `forEach`/`collect` for effects).
java-mod-003.example:
```java
import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

List<String> names = List.of("Ana", "Beto", "Cira", "Ed");

List<String> result = names.stream() // source
    .filter(n -> n.length() > 2)     // intermediate (lazy)
    .map(String::toUpperCase)        // intermediate (lazy)
    .sorted()                        // intermediate (lazy)
    .collect(Collectors.toList());   // terminal -> runs the pipeline

System.out.println(result); // [ANA, BETO, CIRA]
long count = names.stream().filter(n -> n.startsWith("A")).count(); // terminal
```

java-mod-004.explanation: **The problem:** people assume each `filter`/`map` loops over the data immediately, then are surprised that a pipeline with no terminal op does nothing. **Why collect triggers it:** intermediate operations (`filter`, `map`) are *lazy* — they only record what to do and return a new stream. The **terminal** operation (`collect` here) is what actually pulls elements through the entire chain. **Why this is efficient:** because execution is deferred, the elements flow through `filter` then `map` *one at a time in a single pass* (loop fusion), not in separate passes per operation — and short-circuiting terminals like `findFirst`/`anyMatch` can stop early. **The mental model:** building a pipeline (intermediate) vs running it (terminal). **Common mistakes:** forgetting the terminal op (nothing executes); assuming multiple intermediate ops mean multiple passes (it's one pass); and relying on side effects inside intermediates that never run because there's no terminal.

java-mod-005.explanation: **The problem:** returning `null` to mean "no value" is invisible in the type signature, so callers forget to check and get `NullPointerException`s. **What Optional does:** `Optional<T>` makes "might be absent" explicit — a method returning `Optional<User>` forces the caller to acknowledge the empty case. **How to use it well:** prefer the functional methods — `map`/`flatMap` to transform if present, `filter` to drop values, `orElse(default)` / `orElseGet(supplier)` for a fallback, `orElseThrow()` to fail loudly, `ifPresent(consumer)` to act only when present. **Avoid** `if (o.isPresent()) o.get()` — that's just a null check in disguise, and bare `get()` throws if empty. **Where to use it:** as a *return type*; **not** as a field or method parameter (overkill, and it's not serializable-friendly). **Why it works:** the type system carries the maybe-ness, so the compiler and reader can't ignore it. **Common mistakes:** `Optional.of(maybeNull)` (throws — use `ofNullable`); calling `get()` without checking; and wrapping things in Optional everywhere.

java-mod-006.explanation: **The problem:** lambdas that *only* forward their arguments to an existing method (`x -> System.out.println(x)`) are noisy. **What a method reference does:** `Type::method` is shorthand for exactly that lambda, letting you name the method directly. **The four forms:** (1) **static** — `Integer::parseInt` ≡ `s -> Integer.parseInt(s)`. (2) **bound instance** (a specific object) — `System.out::println` ≡ `x -> System.out.println(x)`. (3) **unbound instance** (an arbitrary object of a type, which becomes the first argument) — `String::toUpperCase` ≡ `s -> s.toUpperCase()`. (4) **constructor** — `ArrayList::new` ≡ `() -> new ArrayList<>()`. **Why it works:** the target functional interface determines how the parameters map to the method's receiver/arguments. **Why use it:** more readable and intention-revealing than the equivalent lambda. **Common mistakes:** reaching for a method reference when the lambda does extra work (then a lambda is required); and confusing the unbound form (instance method via the type name) with the static form — both look like `Type::name`.

java-mod-007.explanation: **The problem:** overriding relies on matching the parent method's *exact* signature — one typo and you've accidentally written a brand-new method that never gets called, a bug that's invisible at compile time. **What @Override does:** it's an annotation that declares intent — "this method overrides a supertype method." The compiler then verifies a matching method really exists in a superclass or interface; if not, it errors. **The classic save:** writing `public boolean equals(MyType o)` instead of `equals(Object o)` compiles fine as an *overload* and silently breaks collections — `@Override` turns that into a compile error. **Why it works:** it converts a runtime mystery into a compile-time check, and documents intent for readers. **It's optional but recommended on every override.** **Common mistakes:** omitting it and shipping a broken `equals`/`hashCode`/`toString`; and thinking it *causes* overriding (it doesn't — it only *verifies* it).

java-mod-008.explanation: **The problem:** `NullPointerException` is Java's most common runtime error, and knowing what actually triggers it prevents most of them. **The two real causes here:** (1) **dereferencing null** — calling a method or accessing a field/array element on a reference that is `null` (`s.length()` when `s == null`). (2) **unboxing a null wrapper** — `int n = someInteger;` where the `Integer` is `null` has no value to unbox, so it throws. **Why the others don't:** assigning `null` to a reference variable is perfectly legal; `"x".equals(maybeNull)` is safe because the *receiver* is non-null (it's calling `.equals` *on* a null that would throw); and an uninitialized *local* primitive is a *compile* error, not a runtime NPE (fields default to 0/false). **Why it works to know this:** most NPEs trace to a value you assumed was present but wasn't — guard with null checks, `Optional`, or `Objects.requireNonNull`. **Common mistakes:** chaining calls on possibly-null results; and `map.get(k).something()` when the key is absent.
